Hi doctor, thank you. Well, I guess... it's just been really frustrating lately. I work as a secretary, and I've been doing admin work since high school, so my entire day is usually about keeping things organized for other people. But what finally made me ask for help is that I just keep forgetting little things I normally handle without a problem. 

It's the small stuff, you know? Like, I'll completely forget to return calls, which is ridiculous because I'm sitting right by the phone all day. Or I had this registration form I needed to turn in, and I just... I don't know, it completely slipped my mind even though I knew it was important. And errands are a nightmare right now. I'll plan to stop for an errand on the way home, and I'll think about it all afternoon, but then I just drive straight home and pull into the driveway before I realize I drove right past the place. 

It's just so embarrassing because I'm 36 years old and I should be able to remember to pick up a few things or drop off a simple form. I try to leave myself notes, but then I just walk right past the notes without looking at them. It's making me feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit, to be honest, just constantly dropping the ball on these everyday tasks that shouldn't be this hard. So I just really felt like I needed to come in and figure out what is going on with me.

Well, um... I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly. I mean, I'm definitely not walking around crying all the time or feeling like I can't get out of bed, you know? It's not like that heavy, dark feeling people talk about when they're depressed. And I wouldn't say I'm super anxious in general, like having panic attacks or worrying about everything under the sun.

And when I realize I forgot something *again*, I do get this horrible sinking feeling in my stomach. It's like, "Oh great, what else have I dropped the ball on today?" So I guess there's some anxiety there, but it's very specific to me messing up at work or school. It's not like a general, free-floating anxiety. It's more of a... a dread of the consequences of my own forgetfulness. 

And as for irritable... maybe a little? But again, it's mostly directed at myself. I get so mad at myself when I walk past a note I left on the counter, or when I pull into the driveway and realize I forgot to stop at the pharmacy. I'll just sit in the car and think, "How could you be so stupid?" Sometimes I might snap a little bit if someone interrupts me when I'm trying really, really hard to focus on something so I don't forget it, but I don't think I'm walking around angry at the world. It's just... it's just this constant, underlying frustration with my own brain, you know? It's exhausting having to police yourself all the time and still failing at it. But I don't think it's like a clinical depression or anxiety thing. Just... just being really fed up with myself.

Well, birthdays and stuff... I mean, mostly it's the everyday things. Like I was saying earlier, what really pushed me to finally make an appointment and come in here was just this constant stream of forgetting all these little things I normally handle without any problem at all.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
No, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble learning new things, exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting in my night classes and the professor is speaking Greek. When I'm actually sitting there, paying attention—well, trying to pay attention—and taking notes, the concepts make sense. Like, we're doing this module on organizational behavior right now, which is super relevant for the Office Manager thing, and I get it. I understand the theories and the case studies and all of that. 

The problem isn't the learning part, it's the... the execution part, I guess? It's like I can absorb the information just fine, but then keeping track of what I'm supposed to do with it, or when I'm supposed to do it, is where everything falls apart. Like I said, I'll do all the reading for a new topic, completely understand it, and then totally forget to actually upload the assignment by 11:59 PM. 

And at work, it's the same kind of deal. If my boss shows me a new way to format a report or a new feature in our scheduling software, I pick it up right away. I've always been a quick learner when it comes to admin stuff; you kind of have to be when you're the one holding the office together. But it's just... it's the remembering to *use* the new formatting on the report three days later, or remembering to click that one specific box in the new software when I'm rushing to get a meeting scheduled. 

So, yeah, the actual learning of new skills or facts hasn't really changed. My brain can still comprehend new things. It's just that the new things—and the old things, honestly—just don't seem to stick in my short-term memory long enough for me to actually follow through on them. It's like the filing cabinet in my head is still working, but the receptionist who's supposed to put the files in the right folders keeps going on coffee breaks and leaving the papers scattered all over the desk.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, major life changes... I mean, the biggest thing, the thing that really seems to be the root of all this, is school. I started this evening certificate program about 15 months ago, and honestly, that's when these attention and organization problems became noticeably harder to manage. 

Before that, I was just working. And you know, being an admin assistant, I've got my routines. I go in, I know the drill, I handle the phones, the scheduling, the filing—it's all very structured. I mean, I'm 36, I've been doing this kind of work since I got out of high school, so I have my systems in place. But then, about a year and a quarter ago, I decided I wanted to go for this Office Manager position that was going to be opening up. Our current manager is retiring, and I thought, "This is my chance, I need to step up." But they wanted someone with some formal management training, which I didn't have, just my high school diploma and years of experience. So, I enrolled in this business administration certificate program at the community college.

And it's just... it's been a lot. It's not just the classes themselves, which are two nights a week, but it's the reading, the assignments, the group projects—which, don't even get me started on group projects when you're already struggling to keep your own head above water. Trying to coordinate with three other adults who all work full-time? It's a nightmare. 

So, I'm working 8 to 5, then I'm rushing to class, or I'm rushing home to log onto a virtual lecture, and then I'm up until midnight trying to read textbook chapters on human resources law or whatever. And that's when everything really started slipping. It's like my brain was a sponge that was already full with just my day job, and now I'm trying to pour a whole bucket of water on it, and it's just spilling everywhere. The forgetting the phone calls, the leaving the registration form on my desk, driving past the grocery store—all of that really ramped up after I started the program. 

It's just this constant, overwhelming pressure to perform at work so I look good for the promotion, while also trying to keep my grades up in the certificate program so I actually qualify for the promotion. And I just... I feel like I'm failing at both because I can't keep all the plates spinning anymore. So, yeah, starting that program 15 months ago was a huge change, and it's definitely been the major stressor that's made all these memory and focus issues so much worse.

Forgetting steps for things I've done a lot? Um... no, actually. No, I don't think so. Because, like I was saying earlier, I've been an admin assistant since I was basically eighteen, right out of high school. So the things I do every day, they're really like muscle memory at this point.

I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly. I mean, I'm definitely not walking around crying all the time or feeling like I can't get out of bed, you know? It's not like that heavy, dark feeling people talk about when they're depressed. And I wouldn't say I'm super anxious in general, like having panic attacks or worrying about everything under the sun. \n\nBut, I mean, I *am* stressed. Really stressed. Like I was saying about the Office Manager position—it's just constantly on my mind. And when I realize I forgot something *again*, I do get this horrible sinking feeling in my stomach. It's like, \"Oh great, what else have I dropped the ball on today?\" So I guess there's some anxiety there, but it's very specific to me messing up at work or school. It's not like a general, free-floating anxiety. It's more of a... a dread of the consequences of my own forgetfulness. \n\nAnd as for irritable... maybe a little? But again, it's mostly directed at myself. I get so mad at myself when I walk past a note I left on the counter, or when I pull into the driveway and realize I forgot to stop at the pharmacy. I'll just sit in the car and think, \"How could you be so stupid?\" Sometimes I might snap a little bit if someone interrupts me when I'm trying really, really hard to focus on something so I don't forget it, but I don't think I'm walking around angry at the world. It's just... it's just this constant, underlying frustration with my own brain, you know? It's exhausting having to police yourself all the time and still failing at it. Things from before? Like, my long-term memory? Oh, no, not at all. My long-term memory is actually incredibly sharp. I can remember things from years ago with crystal clarity. 

Like, for instance, I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation—it was this pale yellow dress with little white daisies embroidered along the hem, and I had these terrible strappy sandals that gave me blisters before we even walked across the stage. And it's the same with work stuff from before this whole overwhelmed phase started. I can recall conversations I had with the old regional director three years ago, before he retired and moved to Florida. I remember he always used to ask for his coffee with exactly one and a half packets of Splenda, never two, because two was "too cloying," whatever that means. I remember the exact date we switched over our filing system from the old color-coded folders to the digital database—it was October 14th, four years ago, and it rained that whole week. 

So, no, anything that got filed away in my brain before I started taking these night classes and trying to juggle a million things at once... that stuff is totally secure. It's locked in the vault. It's really just the short-term stuff right now, the things that are happening while my brain is already at maximum capacity, that seem to just bounce right off. If you ask me what I had for dinner last night, I might have to really stop and think about it, but if you ask me about my tenth birthday party at the roller rink? I could tell you the entire playlist and what flavor the cake was. So the old memories are perfectly fine, it's just the new ones that aren't sticking.

I don't know if I'm forgetting birthdays more than usual, because I've always relied on my calendar for that anyway, but it's these little daily tasks, these things I do every single day, that are just slipping right through the cracks. It's like my brain just deletes the information the second I look away.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty learning new things, such as new skills or information, since you started experiencing these memory problems?\n\nPatient: No, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble learning new things, exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting in my night classes and the professor is speaking Greek. When I'm actually sitting there, paying attention—well, trying to pay attention—and taking notes, the concepts make sense. Like, we're doing this module on organizational behavior right now, which is super relevant for the Office Manager thing, and I get it. I understand the theories and the case studies and all of that. \n\nThe problem isn't the learning part, it's the... the execution part, I guess? It's like I can absorb the information just fine, but then keeping track of what I'm supposed to do with it, or when I'm supposed to do it, is where everything falls apart. Like I said, I'll do all the reading for a new topic, completely understand it, and then totally forget to actually upload the assignment by 11:59 PM. \n\nAnd at work, it's the same kind of deal. If my boss shows me a new way to format a report or a new feature in our scheduling software, I pick it up right away. I've always been a quick learner when it comes to admin stuff; you kind of have to be when you're the one holding the office together. But it's just... it's the remembering to *use* the new formatting on the report three days later, or remembering to click that one specific box in the new software when I'm rushing to get a meeting scheduled. \n\nSo, yeah, the actual learning of new skills or facts hasn't really changed. My brain can still comprehend new things. It's just that the new things—and the old things, honestly—just don't seem to stick in my short-term memory long enough for me to actually follow through on them. It's like the filing cabinet in my head is still working, but the receptionist who's supposed to put the files in the right folders keeps going on coffee breaks and leaving the papers scattered all over the desk.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any major life changes or stressful events recently?\n\nPatient: Well, major life changes... I mean, the biggest thing, the thing that really seems to be the root of all this, is school. I started this evening certificate program about 15 months ago, and honestly, that's when these attention and organization problems became noticeably harder to manage. \n\nBefore that, I was just working. And you know, being an admin assistant, I've got my routines. I go in, I know the drill, I handle the phones, the scheduling, the filing—it's all very structured. I mean, I'm 36, I've been doing this kind of work since I got out of high school, so I have my systems in place. But then, about a year and a quarter ago, I decided I wanted to go for this Office Manager position that was going to be opening up. Our current manager is retiring, and I thought, \"This is my chance, I need to step up.\" But they wanted someone with some formal management training, which I didn't have, just my high school diploma and years of experience. So, I enrolled in this business administration certificate program at the community college.\n\nAnd it's just... it's been a lot. It's not just the classes themselves, which are two nights a week, but it's the reading, the assignments, the group projects—which, don't even get me started on group projects when you're already struggling to keep your own head above water. Trying to coordinate with three other adults who all work full-time? It's a nightmare. \n\nSo, I'm working 8 to 5, then I'm rushing to class, or I'm rushing home to log onto a virtual lecture, and then I'm up until midnight trying to read textbook chapters on human resources law or whatever. And that's when everything really started slipping. It's like my brain was a sponge that was already full with just my day job, and now I'm trying to pour a whole bucket of water on it, and it's just spilling everywhere. The forgetting the phone calls, the leaving the registration form on my desk, driving past the grocery store—all of that really ramped up after I started the program. \n\nIt's just this constant, overwhelming pressure to perform at work so I look good for the promotion, while also trying to keep my grades up in the certificate program so I actually qualify for the promotion. And I just... I feel like I'm failing at both because I can't keep all the plates spinning anymore. So, yeah, starting that program 15 months ago was a huge change, and it's definitely been the major stressor that's made all these memory and focus issues so much worse.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your physical health recently?\n\nPatient: Physical health? Well, no, not really. I mean, I'm exhausted, obviously, but I think anyone would be with the schedule I just told you about. You know, working all day and then doing the classes at night, it just completely drains you. But as far as actual health problems, like getting sick or, I don't know, weird pains or anything like that? No. \n\nMy immune system seems to be holding up, thankfully. I haven't even had so much as a cold this year, which is honestly kind of a miracle because usually when the seasons change, I get this terrible sinus thing that just knocks me out for a week. The office air conditioning is always blasting, and people come in coughing and touching the pens on my desk... but yeah, physically I'm fine. \n\nI do try to make sure I'm at least drinking enough water, even if my diet has kind of devolved into whatever I can grab from the vending machine or the drive-thru between work and my evening lectures. I know I should probably be eating better, maybe making salads or something, but who has the time to meal prep when you're forgetting to even buy the groceries in the first place, right? Like I was saying with the dry cleaning, if I can't even remember to pull into the store, I'm definitely not chopping vegetables. \n\nSo, yeah, aside from just the general exhaustion of burning the candle at both ends and maybe not eating the greatest right now, my actual physical health hasn't changed at all. My blood pressure was totally fine at my last checkup, and I don't have any new physical issues. It really is just my brain that feels like it's completely malfunctioning.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting things even when you're relaxed and not feeling overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: Relaxed? Gosh, um... I kind of have to search my memory for the last time I actually felt relaxed! With the 8 to 5 job and the evening classes, \"relaxed\" isn't exactly in my vocabulary right now. But... if I really think about it, like, maybe during the two-week break I had between the fall and spring semesters? \n\nDuring those two weeks, I didn't have any reading to do, no group projects to coordinate, and the office was actually pretty quiet because half the staff takes time off around the holidays. And you know what? No, I don't think I was forgetting things then. When I actually have real downtime, and I'm just... existing, without a million mental tabs open, my brain seems to function just fine. \n\nLike, during that break, I remembered to water my plants, I remembered to call my mom back—which she was thrilled about, because usually I see her name pop up on my phone, think \"Oh, I'll call her after my lecture,\" and then completely blank on it for three days. But when the pressure is off and I'm not feeling completely buried under all the schedules and deadlines, I don't really have these memory blanks. \n\nIt's like my brain only short-circuits when the system is overloaded. If I'm just sitting on the couch on a Sunday morning, drinking coffee and not worrying about whether I formatted the weekly executive report right or if I studied enough for my HR quiz, I don't find myself walking into a room and forgetting why I went in there. It's just that, right now, the juggling never really stops. Even when I try to take a bath or watch a show to unwind, I'm usually just making a mental list of what I have to do the next day, so I'm not *truly* relaxed anyway. But yeah, when I actually am? No, the forgetting doesn't really happen.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting steps or details when doing tasks you've done many times before?\n\nPatient: Forgetting steps for things I've done a lot? I never forget to log them. It's just... boom, boom, boom, done. I don't even really have to think about it.\n\nOr like, the weekly executive summary reports. I've been formatting those for our current office manager for, gosh, five years now? I don't forget those details because they're just hardwired into my brain at this point. If I was forgetting how to do my basic job, I wouldn't even be trying for the promotion, you know? It's just... when I step out of that routine, or when my brain gets yanked away by, say, suddenly remembering I have a human resources quiz at 7 PM, that's when things get messy. But the actual steps of my normal routine? No, I never miss a step there.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble remembering things that happened before you started experiencing these memory problems?\n\nPatient: Things from before? I can remember the exact layout of my childhood bedroom, down to where my mom hung this weird macrame owl she bought at a craft fair in 1996. I can even remember the phone number of my best friend from middle school, 555-0198, even though I haven't dialed it in probably twenty years! \n\nAnd it's the same with work stuff from before this whole overwhelmed phase started. I can recall conversations I had with the old regional director three years ago, before he retired and moved to Florida. Pressure to perform? Um... you mean like, stage fright, or having a boss breathe down my neck? 

Actually, no, I haven't really noticed that being a trigger. It's kind of funny, because you'd think that would be the case, right? It's not like a general, free-floating anxiety. It's more of a... a dread of the consequences of my own forgetfulness. \n\nAnd as for irritable... maybe a little? It's just... it's just this constant, underlying frustration with my own brain, you know? It's exhausting having to police yourself all the time and still failing at it. It's like my brain just deletes the information the second I look away.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty learning new things, such as new skills or information, since you started experiencing these memory problems?\n\nPatient: No, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble learning new things, exactly. Doing multiple things at the same time? Um... no, not really. I mean, honestly, I'm practically the queen of multitasking. You kind of have to be when you're an administrative assistant, right?

So no, I don't think doing things simultaneously is what makes me forget. The actual physical act of doing three things at once at my desk? I'm totally fine with that. I don't drop the ball when I'm actively juggling in the moment. It's really just... like I was saying before, it's having too many overarching responsibilities taking up space in my brain long-term, like knowing I have to read three chapters for my HR class by Thursday, and also remembering to pay the electric bill, and also remembering that the cat needs her flea medication. It's the background stuff that gets lost. But actively multitasking in the present moment? No, that doesn't seem to trigger the memory blanks at all. That's exactly why I know I'd be a great Office Manager, because I have all these systems completely locked down. If I was forgetting how to do my basic job, I wouldn't even be trying for the promotion, you know? It's just... when I step out of that routine, or when my brain gets yanked away by, say, suddenly remembering I have a human resources quiz at 7 PM, that's when things get messy. But the actual steps of my normal routine? No, I never miss a step there.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble remembering things that happened before you started experiencing these memory problems?\n\nPatient: Things from before? Like, my long-term memory? Oh, no, not at all. My long-term memory is actually incredibly sharp. I can remember things from years ago with crystal clarity. \n\nLike, for instance, I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation—it was this pale yellow dress with little white daisies embroidered along the hem, and I had these terrible strappy sandals that gave me blisters before we even walked across the stage. I can remember the exact layout of my childhood bedroom, down to where my mom hung this weird macrame owl she bought at a craft fair in 1996. I can even remember the phone number of my best friend from middle school, 555-0198, even though I haven't dialed it in probably twenty years! \n\nAnd it's the same with work stuff from before this whole overwhelmed phase started. I can recall conversations I had with the old regional director three years ago, before he retired and moved to Florida. I remember he always used to ask for his coffee with exactly one and a half packets of Splenda, never two, because two was \"too cloying,\" whatever that means. I remember the exact date we switched over our filing system from the old color-coded folders to the digital database—it was October 14th, four years ago, and it rained that whole week. \n\nSo, no, anything that got filed away in my brain before I started taking these night classes and trying to juggle a million things at once... that stuff is totally secure. It's locked in the vault. It's really just the short-term stuff right now, the things that are happening while my brain is already at maximum capacity, that seem to just bounce right off. If you ask me what I had for dinner last night, I might have to really stop and think about it, but if you ask me about my tenth birthday party at the roller rink? I could tell you the entire playlist and what flavor the cake was. So the old memories are perfectly fine, it's just the new ones that aren't sticking.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your memory problems are triggered or made worse when you're under a lot of pressure to perform?\n\nPatient: Pressure to perform? Um... you mean like, stage fright, or having a boss breathe down my neck? \n\nActually, no, I haven't really noticed that being a trigger. It's kind of funny, because you'd think that would be the case, right? But if I'm, say, taking one of my HR exams for my evening classes—which is definitely high pressure because I absolutely have to keep a B average if I want the company to reimburse my tuition at the end of the semester—I don't sit there and blank out on what I studied. I actually do pretty well on the tests themselves. \n\nOr like at work, if my office manager is standing right over my desk waiting for me to pull a specific vendor contract for a sudden meeting with the regional VP, I don't suddenly forget how our filing system works or where I put the folder. If anything, when there's that kind of direct, immediate pressure to perform, it's almost like my brain snaps into focus. I get this little rush of adrenaline and I just handle it. I've always been pretty good in a pinch. Like just last month, our main copier jammed right before a massive quarterly review meeting, and I had to manually collate and staple thirty packets in about five minutes while three different executives were pacing around the lobby. High pressure, definitely! But I didn't forget what I was doing or miss any pages, I just got it done. \n\nSo, no, I don't think it's the pressure to perform a specific task that makes me forget things. It's not performance anxiety or anything like that. Like I was saying before, it's really just the sheer volume of everything. It's when I have twenty completely mundane, low-pressure things floating around in my head—like remembering to buy cat food, and emailing the janitorial staff about the paper towels, and reading chapter four... that's when things slip through the cracks. But when all eyes are on me to do one important thing? No, I don't really have memory blanks then. The pressure almost helps, honestly. I know some people completely freeze up when they're put on the spot, like my sister, she completely bombs job interviews because of the pressure, but for me, that's really not when the forgetting happens.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it difficult to remember where you left off when you have to switch between different tasks or activities?\n\nPatient: Switching tasks? And remembering where I left off? Um... no, actually, I don't really have a problem with that. Which is lucky, because being an administrative assistant, my entire day is basically just one long string of interruptions. If I couldn't remember where I left off, I'd never get a single thing done! \n\nLike, just to give you an idea of a normal Tuesday... I'll be right in the middle of typing up an email to our property management company because the air conditioning in the breakroom is making that horrible rattling noise again—which, honestly, happens every single summer like clockwork, you'd think they would just replace the main unit instead of sending the same maintenance guy, Gary, out to put a band-aid on it every July—but anyway, I'll be mid-sentence on that email, and then the multi-line phone will start ringing. I just stop, walk them down the hall, make some small talk about the traffic on I-95, and then walk right back to the copier and finish putting the cartridge in. I don't stand there wondering why my hands are covered in black ink, you know? It's really only when I'm trying to juggle all the new stuff, like the human resources classes and the studying on top of the normal life stuff, that my brain just sort of... hits a wall and drops things. But just switching from one normal task to another and going back again? No, I never lose my place with that. I'm actually really proud of how well I handle the front desk chaos, to be honest. If I couldn't bounce back from an interruption, our office manager would have replaced me years ago!\n\nDoctor: Do you find that you forget things more often when you're trying to do multiple things at the same time?\n\nPatient: Doing multiple things at the same time? You kind of have to be when you're an administrative assistant, right? \n\nLike, just to give you an example, yesterday around noon I was on the phone with the Poland Spring water delivery guy—because they keep leaving the five-gallon jugs in the wrong hallway, right by the emergency exit, which is a massive fire hazard and I've told their dispatch office at least three times about it this month alone—but anyway, I was on the phone with him, while simultaneously typing up the minutes from the morning staff meeting, and eating my turkey and swiss sandwich. And I didn't forget what I was typing, and I didn't forget the point I was trying to make to the dispatcher, and I didn't accidentally type my lunch order into the meeting minutes! \n\nI actually kind of thrive when I have three different things going on at once. It's almost like a dance, you know? I can be transferring a call on line one, signing a clipboard for a UPS package with my right hand, and waving a visitor toward the waiting area with my left hand, all in the exact same ten seconds. My old boss, Mr. Henderson—the one who moved to Florida—he used to say I was like an octopus, just managing eight different things at once without even breaking a sweat. \n\nSo no, I don't think doing things simultaneously is what makes me forget. The actual physical act of doing three things at once at my desk? I'm totally fine with that. I don't drop the ball when I'm actively juggling in the moment. It's really just... like I was saying before, it's having too many overarching responsibilities taking up space in my brain long-term, like knowing I have to read three chapters for my HR class by Thursday, and also remembering to pay the electric bill, and also remembering that the cat needs her flea medication. I can even remember the phone number of my best friend from middle school, 555-0198, even though I haven't dialed it in probably twenty years! \n\nAnd it's the same with work stuff from before this whole overwhelmed phase started. I remember he always used to ask for his coffee with exactly one and a half packets of Splenda, never two, because two was \"too cloying,\" whatever that means. It's locked in the vault. It's really just the short-term stuff right now, the things that are happening while my brain is already at maximum capacity, that seem to just bounce right off. If you ask me what I had for dinner last night, I might have to really stop and think about it, but if you ask me about my tenth birthday party at the roller rink? I could tell you the entire playlist and what flavor the cake was. Um... you mean like, stage fright, or having a boss breathe down my neck? \n\nActually, no, I haven't really noticed that being a trigger. It's kind of funny, because you'd think that would be the case, right? I actually do pretty well on the tests themselves. \n\nOr like at work, if my office manager is standing right over my desk waiting for me to pull a specific vendor contract for a sudden meeting with the regional VP, I don't suddenly forget how our filing system works or where I put the folder. If anything, when there's that kind of direct, immediate pressure to perform, it's almost like my brain snaps into focus. I get this little rush of adrenaline and I just handle it. I've always been pretty good in a pinch. Remembering what happened yesterday? Or the day before? Um, no, not really. I mean, I remember the big stuff, the actual events of the day, you know? Like, I can tell you exactly what happened yesterday. 

Yesterday was Tuesday, so it was our weekly staff meeting in the morning, which was... well, it was exactly as tedious as it always is. Gary spent twenty minutes talking about the new protocol for the toner cartridges, which we all already know because he sent out an email about it last Thursday with a PDF attachment that I had to print out and put in everyone's mailboxes. And then after the meeting, I had my usual lunch—I always bring a turkey sandwich on Tuesdays because I roast a turkey breast on Sundays, and Tuesday is when it's still good but I need to finish it before it gets weird. I ate it at my desk while I was trying to catch up on the emails I missed during the meeting. 

And then the day before yesterday, Monday, was just... Monday. You know how Mondays are. The phones were crazy because everyone was calling about things they thought of over the weekend. Oh!
